{{Short description|Sporadic simple group}}
{{for|general background and history of the Janko sporadic groups|Janko group}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Janko group J<sub>3</sub>}}
{{Group theory sidebar |Finite}}

In the area of modern algebra known as [[group theory]], the '''Janko group''' ''J<sub>3</sub>'' or the '''Higman-Janko-McKay group''' ''HJM'' is a [[sporadic simple group]] of [[Order (group theory)|order]]
:&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;50,232,960 = 2<sup>7</sup>{{·}}3<sup>5</sup>{{·}}5{{·}}17{{·}}19.

==History and properties==
''J<sub>3</sub>'' is one of the 26 [[Sporadic group]]s and was predicted by [[Zvonimir Janko]] in 1969 as one of two new simple groups having  2<sup>1+4</sup>:A<sub>5</sub> as a centralizer of an involution (the other is the Janko group [[Janko group J2|''J<sub>2</sub>'']]). 
''J<sub>3</sub>'' was shown to exist by {{harvs|txt |author1-link=Graham Higman |first=Graham |last=Higman |author2-link=John McKay (mathematician) |first2=John |last2=McKay |year=1969}}.

In 1982 [[R. L. Griess]] showed that ''J<sub>3</sub>'' cannot be a [[subquotient]] of the [[monster group]].<ref>Griess (1982): p. 93: proof that  J<sub>3</sub> is a pariah.</ref>  Thus it is one of the 6 sporadic groups called the [[pariah group|pariahs]].

J<sub>3</sub> has an [[outer automorphism group]] of order 2 and a  [[Schur multiplier]] of order 3, and its triple cover has a unitary 9-dimensional [[Modular representation theory|representation]] over the [[finite field]] with 4 elements. {{harvtxt|Weiss|1982}} constructed it via an underlying geometry. It has a modular representation of dimension eighteen over the [[finite field]] with 9 elements.
It has a complex projective representation of dimension eighteen.

The degrees of [[irreducible representation|irreducible representations]] of the Janko group ''J<sub>3</sub>'' are 1, 85, 85, 323, 323, 324,&nbsp;... {{OEIS|id=A003906}}.

=== Using the subgroup PSL(2,16) ===
The automorphism group ''J''<sub>3</sub>:2 can be constructed by starting with the subgroup PSL(2,16):4 and adjoining 120 involutions, which are identified with the [[Sylow theorems|Sylow]] 17-subgroups. Note that these 120 involutions are outer elements of ''J''<sub>3</sub>:2. One then defines the following relation:

<math>\left(\begin{matrix}1&1\\1&0\end{matrix}\sigma t_{(\nu,\nu7)}\right)^5=1</math>

where <math>\sigma</math> is the [[Frobenius endomorphism|Frobenius automorphism]] of order 4, and <math>t_{(\nu,\nu7)}</math> is the unique 17-cycle that sends

<math>\infty\rightarrow0\rightarrow1\rightarrow7</math>

Curtis showed, using a computer, that this relation is sufficient to define ''J''<sub>3</sub>:2.<ref>{{citation| title=Symmetric Generationand existence of ''J''<sub>3</sub>:2, the automorphism group of the third Janko group| last1=Bradley | first1=J.D. | last2=Curtis | first2=R.T. | doi=10.1016/j.jalgebra.2005.09.046 |journal=Journal of Algebra | volume=304 | issue=1 | year=2006| pages=256–270 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

=== Using a presentation ===

In terms of generators ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', and ''d'' its automorphism group J<sub>3</sub>:2 can be [[Presentation of a group|presented]] as
<math>a^{17} = b^8 = a^ba^{-2} = c^2 = b^cb^3 = (abc)^4 = (ac)^{17} = d^2 = [d, a] = [d, b] = (a^3b^{-3}cd)^5 = 1.</math>

A presentation for J<sub>3</sub> in terms of (different) generators ''a'', ''b'', ''c'', ''d'' is
<math>a^{19} = b^9 = a^ba^2 = c^2 = d^2 = (bc)^2 = (bd)^2 = (ac)^3 = (ad)^3 = (a^2ca^{-3}d)^3 = 1.</math>
